binders: A finite index range i=1,...,N (with the nonempty range implicit in the displayed maximum defining K).
Real random variables X_1,...,X_N on a common probability space.
A real coefficient vector a=(a_1,...,a_N) in R^N.
A real exponent p satisfying 0 < p < 2.
The sub-gaussian size parameter K = max_i ||X_i||_{psi_2}.
hypotheses: The X_i are independent (Exercise 2.6.5, inherited through the adjacent low-moment exercises on PDF page 19 / printed page 30).
Each X_i is sub-gaussian (Exercise 2.6.5, same location).
Each X_i has mean zero and variance one (Exercise 2.6.5, same location).
The exponent is in the open interval (0,2), including the quasi-norm range 0<p<1 (Exercise 2.6.7 title and text, same location).
conclusions: The reader must state and prove a Khintchine-type low-moment estimate for ||sum_i a_i X_i||_{L^p} when 0<p<2.

Read together with Exercises 2.6.5 and 2.6.6, the intended mathematical content is a two-sided comparison of ||sum_i a_i X_i||_{L^p} with (sum_i a_i^2)^(1/2), with constants uniform in N, the coefficient vector, and the particular family once its allowed parameters are fixed.

A natural source-consistent formulation is c(K,p) (sum_i a_i^2)^(1/2) <= ||sum_i a_i X_i||_{L^p} <= (sum_i a_i^2)^(1/2) for some c(K,p)>0; this formula reconstructs the intended 'version' from the neighboring displays and hint, because Exercise 2.6.7 itself does not print or uniquely prescribe it.
definitions_and_conventions: K denotes max_i ||X_i||_{psi_2}, as explicitly defined in Exercises 2.6.5 and 2.6.6 on PDF page 19 / printed page 30.
||sum_i a_i X_i||_{L^p} is the L^p size used throughout the three adjacent Khintchine exercises; for 0<p<1 the source still includes the exponent even though this is only a quasi-norm.
The coefficient scale is the Euclidean quantity (sum_i a_i^2)^(1/2), as displayed in Exercises 2.6.5 and 2.6.6.
An 'absolute constant' is explicitly used in Exercise 2.6.5, whereas Exercise 2.6.7 leaves the constants in the requested version unstated.
implicit_context: Exercise 2.6.7 does not repeat its probabilistic setting; its title, adjacency, and explicit instruction to modify Exercise 2.6.6's extrapolation trick connect it to the setting of Exercise 2.6.5.
The p=1 result in Exercise 2.6.6 is the model low-moment statement, and its hint uses the high-moment p=3 case of Exercise 2.6.5.
The requested result is uniform over the finite dimension N and coefficients a, as is the form of both preceding exercises.

details: Cover every exponent strictly between 0 and 2 in the independent, centered, unit-variance sub-gaussian setting inherited from Exercise 2.6.5.
Give a genuine Khintchine comparison at the Euclidean coefficient scale, not merely an unrelated moment estimate.
Provide both the statement and its proof; the prescribed proof guidance is to modify the extrapolation argument from Exercise 2.6.6.
Exercise 2.6.7 supplies no displayed inequality and no formula for a lower comparison factor.
A positive factor depending only on K and p is the closest analogue of Exercise 2.6.6, but its exact expression and normalization are choices to be justified rather than source literals.

The exact upper coefficient is likewise not restated in Exercise 2.6.7; coefficient 1 is supported by the neighboring p=1 display and the standard low-moment comparison, but is not textually mandated by the selected sentence alone.
The version should apply to arbitrary p in (0,2), arbitrary real coefficients, and any finite family satisfying the inherited assumptions.
Comparison constants must not depend on N, the individual coefficients, or further undisclosed features of the random variables; dependence on K and p is source-consistent.
The stated range excludes p=0 and p=2.
The exercise includes p=1 and exponents below 1; a formulation restricted to 1<=p<2 would omit part of the printed range.
The hint points to interpolation/extrapolation involving an L^2 scale and a higher controlled moment, by analogy with the explicit L^1-L^2-L^3 relation in Exercise 2.6.6.
The hint guides proof construction but does not add a separately asserted theorem or fix a unique closed-form constant.

undebatable_constraints: The exponent range is exactly the open interval 0<p<2; neither endpoint is part of Exercise 2.6.7.
The inherited random variables are independent, sub-gaussian, mean zero, and variance one, with real coefficients a in R^N.
The relevant coefficient scale is (sum_i a_i^2)^(1/2), and K is max_i ||X_i||_{psi_2}.
The exercise is intentionally open-ended: it asks the reader to state a version before proving it and does not print a unique theorem statement.
The hint requires modifying the extrapolation trick of Exercise 2.6.6; it does not specify an exact quantitative lower coefficient.
Any accepted reconstruction must be uniform in N and a and must not silently discard the subrange 0<p<1.

contract_plain_english: Exercise 2.6.7 deliberately asks the reader to formulate, then prove, a low-moment Khintchine inequality rather than supplying a fixed displayed proposition. In the setting inherited through Exercises 2.6.5 and 2.6.6, X_1,...,X_N are independent centered unit-variance sub-gaussian real random variables, a is a real coefficient vector, and K is the largest psi_2 norm. For every 0<p<2, the intended result compares the L^p size of sum_i a_i X_i on both sides with the Euclidean coefficient norm. A natural formulation has a positive lower factor c(K,p) and upper factor 1, but the exact factor, exponent, and normalization are formalizer choices rather than literal source data. The result must remain uniform in the dimension and coefficients and must include the quasi-norm range 0<p<1.
